bibl.title: RIFLE criteria for acute kidney injury are associated with hospital mortality in critically ill patients: a cohort analysis

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: A CLASSIFICATION BEING TESTED AGAINST THE OUTCOME IT CLASSIFIES - 5,383 ICU patients staged by RIFLE, a consensus definition built to replace the more than 30 definitions of acute kidney injury then in use
span.quote: Yet there is no consensus on the amount of dysfunction that defines acute kidney injury, with more than 30 definitions in use in the literature today [ 3 ]. The variety of definitions used in clinical studies may be partly responsible for the large variations in the reported incidence (1–31%) [ 4 - 6 ] and the associated mortality (19–83%) [ 3 , 6 - 9 ] of acute kidney injury.

span.label: does acute kidney injury as defined by the RIFLE classification predict hospital mortality, do patients progress between its classes, and is the classification usable in a general ICU population
span.quote: To establish a uniform definition for acute kidney injury, the Acute Dialysis Quality Initiative formulated the Risk, Injury, Failure, Loss, and End-stage Kidney (RIFLE) classification [ 11 ]. RIFLE defines three grades of increasing severity of acute kidney injury – risk (class R), injury (class I) and failure (class F) – and two outcome classes (loss and end-stage kidney disease)

span.label: the first validation of RIFLE in a large general ICU cohort: incidence 67.2%, mortality rising across classes R/I/F, and class I identified as the stage at which adjusted mortality risk begins
span.quote: The RIFLE classification is a very sensitive definition of acute kidney injury: acute kidney injury defined by the RIFLE classification occurred in two thirds of general ICU patients.

span.label: existence
span.quote: The RIFLE classification is a very sensitive definition of acute kidney injury: acute kidney injury defined by the RIFLE classification occurred in two thirds of general ICU patients.

span.label: a disease whose measured frequency and lethality are properties of the definition chosen for it
span.quote: Yet there is no consensus on the amount of dysfunction that defines acute kidney injury, with more than 30 definitions in use in the literature today [ 3 ]. The variety of definitions used in clinical studies may be partly responsible for the large variations in the reported incidence (1–31%) [ 4 - 6 ] and the associated mortality (19–83%) [ 3 , 6 - 9 ] of acute kidney injury.

span.label: retrospective cohort study of 5,383 ICU patients in seven ICUs, classified by maximum RIFLE class, with covariate-adjusted Cox regression on hospital mortality
span.term: retrospective cohort study of 5,383 ICU patients in seven ICUs, classified by maximum RIFLE class, with covariate-adjusted Cox regression on hospital mortality
span.quote: The RIFLE class was determined based on the worst of either glomerular filtration rate criteria or urine output criteria.

span.label: THE DEFINITION IS THE VARIABLE, AND THE PAPER PUTS A NUMBER ON IT: `there is no consensus on the amount of dysfunction that defines acute kidney injury, with MORE THAN 30 DEFINITIONS IN USE IN THE LITERATURE TODAY. The variety of definitions used in clinical studies MAY BE PARTLY RESPONSIBLE FOR THE LARGE VARIATIONS in the reported INCIDENCE (1-31%) and the associated MORTALITY (19-83%)`. Thirty-one-fold in how often it happens, four-fold in how often it kills
span.quote: Yet there is no consensus on the amount of dysfunction that defines acute kidney injury, with more than 30 definitions in use in the literature today [ 3 ]. The variety of definitions used in clinical studies may be partly responsible for the large variations in the reported incidence (1–31%) [ 4 - 6 ] and the associated mortality (19–83%) [ 3 , 6 - 9 ] of acute kidney injury.

span.label: and what was missing was not the disease but the RULER: `there has not been a consensus on how best to assess kidney function; namely, WHAT MARKERS BEST REFLECT KIDNEY FUNCTION, AND WHAT VALUES OF THOSE MARKERS DISCRIMINATE NORMAL FROM ABNORMAL`. Which quantity, and which cut point on it - the two questions this project calls a threshold
span.quote: Until recently there has not been a consensus on how best to assess kidney function; namely, what markers best reflect kidney function, and what values of those markers discriminate normal from abnormal kidney function.

span.label: THE CLASSIFICATION FIXES BOTH AT ONCE: three severity grades `risk (class R), injury (class I) and failure (class F)` plus `TWO OUTCOME CLASSES (loss and end-stage kidney disease)`. Severity and outcome in one acronym, and this study evaluates only the first three
span.quote: To establish a uniform definition for acute kidney injury, the Acute Dialysis Quality Initiative formulated the Risk, Injury, Failure, Loss, and End-stage Kidney (RIFLE) classification [ 11 ]. RIFLE defines three grades of increasing severity of acute kidney injury – risk (class R), injury (class I) and failure (class F) – and two outcome classes (loss and end-stage kidney disease)

span.label: AND THE PAPER TESTS WHETHER THE VOCABULARY'S WORDS MATCH WHAT ITS CLASSES DO: `RIFLE class R WOULD APPEAR TO BE APTLY NAMED. More than one-half of the patients of class R progressed to more severe RIFLE classes ... RIFLE class I MAY ALSO HAVE BEEN FORTUITOUSLY NAMED, for this is the stage at which risk for hospital mortality increases even after controlling for covariates.` A validation of names, not only of cut points
span.quote: RIFLE class R would appear to be aptly named. More than one-half of the patients of class R progressed to more severe RIFLE classes, yet those that did not were not at increased risk of hospital mortality. Future studies could target this population for prevention. RIFLE class I may also have been fortuitously named, for this is the stage at which risk for hospital mortality increases even after controlling for covariates.

span.label: and the definition creates the epidemiology it is then judged against: `The incidence of ALMOST 70% MAY APPEAR AT ODDS WITH THE EXISTING LITERATURE ... our study highlights the potential for UNDER-REPORTING WHEN RENAL REPLACEMENT THERAPY IS USED TO 'DEFINE' ACUTE KIDNEY INJURY`. A rival operational definition named as the cause of a different number
span.quote: The incidence of almost 70% may appear at odds with the existing literature [ 5 ]. Even when limiting cases to those with RIFLE class F (28%) we found a higher rate for ICU patients than typically reported. Fourteen percent of class F patients received renal replacement therapy, however, leading to a rate of 4–5% among ICU patients, consistent with previous reports [ 9 , 19 ]. Indeed, our study highlights the potential for under-reporting when renal replacement therapy is used to 'define' acute kidney injury.

span.label: THE FIELD'S OWN VERDICT ON WHAT DEFINITIONAL MULTIPLICITY COSTS, WITH A CITATION: `Indeed, THE LACK OF A UNIFORM DEFINITION for acute kidney injury IS BELIEVED TO BE A MAJOR IMPEDIMENT TO RESEARCH IN THE FIELD.` The preceding sentences give the size of it - more than 30 definitions in use, a reported incidence spanning 1-31% and a reported mortality spanning 19-83%. THIS IS THE ONLY PLACE IN THE CORPUS WHERE THE COST OF COMPETING DEFINITIONS IS PUT AS A RANGE ON A MEASURED QUANTITY.
span.quote: Indeed, the lack of a uniform definition for acute kidney injury is believed to be a major impediment to research in the field

span.label: THE DEFINITION REQUIRES AN INPUT THAT OFTEN DOES NOT EXIST, SO IT INVENTS ONE: `The Acute Dialysis Quality Initiative recommended the use of a baseline serum creatinine, yet A TRUE BASELINE IS OFTEN UNKNOWN for patients admitted to the ICU` - so the baseline was computed `by SOLVING THE MDRD EQUATION for serum creatinine ASSUMING a glomerular filtration rate of 75 ml/minute/1.73 m 2`, and `APPROXIMATELY ONE-HALF OF PATIENTS WERE CLASSIFIED USING THE Cr MDRD AS A BASELINE`
span.quote: For patients without chronic kidney insufficiency as reported in the medical history, we calculated a serum creatinine level using the MDRD equation [ 16 ] (Cr MDRD ) as recommended by the Acute Dialysis Quality Initiative, by solving the MDRD equation for serum creatinine assuming a glomerular filtration rate of 75 ml/minute/1.73 m 2 . We then used the lowest creatinine value among the hospital admission creatinine, the ICU admission creatinine or the Cr MDRD creatinine as the baseline value. Approximately one-half of patients were classified using the Cr MDRD as a baseline.

span.label: and the authors name the direction of the bias that choice introduces: `Our use of the LOWEST of these values for any given patient MAY HAVE LEAD TO A HIGHER ESTIMATE OF CHANGE AND THEREFORE A HIGHER ESTIMATE OF THE INCIDENCE of acute kidney injury`. The rule for filling a missing value moves the headline number
span.quote: The Acute Dialysis Quality Initiative recommended the use of a baseline serum creatinine, yet a true baseline is often unknown for patients admitted to the ICU. Several possible baseline values existed for our patients (hospital admission, ICU admission, or a calculated baseline from the MDRD equation). Our use of the lowest of these values for any given patient may have lead to a higher estimate of change and therefore a higher estimate of the incidence of acute kidney injury.

span.label: ONE CLASS LABEL, TWO OPERATIONALISATIONS, DIFFERENT MORTALITY: `Patients with maximum RIFLE class F BASED ON GLOMERULAR FILTRATION RATE CRITERIA had a somewhat higher inhospital mortality compared with patients who had a maximum RIFLE class F ON URINE OUTPUT CRITERIA (27.9% VERSUS 21.9%, P = 0.020)`. The classification declares them equivalent by construction - `the worst of either` - and the outcome says otherwise
span.quote: Patients with maximum RIFLE class F based on glomerular filtration rate criteria had a somewhat higher inhospital mortality compared with patients who had a maximum RIFLE class F on urine output criteria (27.9% versus 21.9%, P = 0.020).

span.label: and the authors say the merge destroys information: `It is possible that URINE OUTPUT AND CREATININE CRITERIA PROVIDE COMPLEMENTARY INFORMATION, WHICH IS LOST WHEN THESE CRITERIA ARE COMBINED`
span.quote: First, we did not attempt to compare RIFLE with other classification systems; nor did we compare urine output and creatinine criteria, but rather used the criteria as proposed by the Acute Dialysis Quality Initiative workgroup, as the worst classification by each criterion. It is possible that urine output and creatinine criteria provide complementary information, which is lost when these criteria are combined.

span.label: THE MEASUREMENT INTERVAL MANUFACTURES A CLASS TRANSITION THAT DID NOT HAPPEN: `our assessment of time to progression ... may have been ARTIFICIALLY LENGTHENED DUE TO DAILY MEASUREMENT OF CREATININE - some patients APPEARED TO SKIP class R or class I`. The sampling rate of the instrument is visible in the patient's trajectory
span.quote: Indeed, our assessment of time to progression of acute kidney injury may have been artificially lengthened due to daily measurement of creatinine – some patients appeared to skip class R or class I because of this limitation.

span.label: and the same artefact is declared in the figure caption, from the other side: `Patients who appear to skip a grade ... do so because THEY DID NOT REMAIN AT A TRANSITION STATE FOR AT LEAST 24 HOURS` - the 24-hour sustained clause in the definition, showing up as missing stages
span.quote: Patients who appear to skip a grade (class risk or class injury) do so because they did not remain at a transition state for at least 24 hours.

span.label: THE DEFINERS VALIDATED THEIR OWN DEFINITION AND SAID SO: `We also acknowledge that SOME MEMBERS OF OUR RESEARCH GROUP HAVE CONTRIBUTED TO THE CONSENSUS PROCESS BY WHICH RIFLE WAS DEVELOPED and by which MDRD recommendations were made`
span.quote: We also acknowledge that some members of our research group have contributed to the consensus process by which RIFLE was developed and by which MDRD recommendations were made.

span.label: and two of the five classes were never tested: `We did not evaluate the OUTCOME CLASSES of RIFLE (loss and end-stage kidney disease criteria) in this study`. The acronym has five letters; the validation covers three
span.quote: We did not evaluate the outcome classes of RIFLE (loss and end-stage kidney disease criteria) in this study.

span.label: the nonrenal SOFA score entered as a covariate instead of the total SOFA score
span.note: eliminates: multicollinearity between the RIFLE class and severity scores that already award points for kidney insufficiency - the outcome scale containing the exposure being tested · outcome: held
span.quote: The RIFLE classification is a very sensitive definition of acute kidney injury: acute kidney injury defined by the RIFLE classification occurred in two thirds of general ICU patients.

span.label: three candidate baseline creatinine values (hospital admission, ICU admission, MDRD-derived), with the lowest taken
span.note: eliminates: nothing, on the authors' own account - it is a rule for filling a missing value, and they state its direction: `MAY HAVE LEAD TO A HIGHER ESTIMATE OF CHANGE AND THEREFORE A HIGHER ESTIMATE OF THE INCIDENCE` · outcome: failed
span.quote: The Acute Dialysis Quality Initiative recommended the use of a baseline serum creatinine, yet a true baseline is often unknown for patients admitted to the ICU. Several possible baseline values existed for our patients (hospital admission, ICU admission, or a calculated baseline from the MDRD equation). Our use of the lowest of these values for any given patient may have lead to a higher estimate of change and therefore a higher estimate of the incidence of acute kidney injury.

span.label: the two RIFLE outcome classes, loss and end-stage kidney disease
span.note: eliminates: nothing here - they were outside the follow-up window and were not assessed · outcome: absent-declared-unreported
span.quote: We did not evaluate the outcome classes of RIFLE (loss and end-stage kidney disease criteria) in this study.

Acute kidney injury should be both abrupt (within 1–7 days) and sustained (more than 24 hours).

span.quote: RIFLE class is determined based on the worst of either glomerular filtration criteria or urine output criteria. span.label: `acute kidney injury` - AT THE TIME OF WRITING, MORE THAN 30 COMPETING SENSES: `no consensus on the amount of dysfunction that defines acute kidney injury, with MORE THAN 30 DEFINITIONS IN USE IN THE LITERATURE TODAY`, and the reported incidence (1-31%) and mortality (19-83%) vary with them
span.quote: Yet there is no consensus on the amount of dysfunction that defines acute kidney injury, with more than 30 definitions in use in the literature today [ 3 ]. The variety of definitions used in clinical studies may be partly responsible for the large variations in the reported incidence (1–31%) [ 4 - 6 ] and the associated mortality (19–83%) [ 3 , 6 - 9 ] of acute kidney injury.

span.label: `acute kidney injury (RIFLE sense)` - meeting ANY of the RIFLE criteria: serum creatinine risen 1.5x, 2x or 3x from baseline, OR urine output below a stated rate for a stated number of hours, `both ABRUPT (WITHIN 1-7 DAYS) AND SUSTAINED (MORE THAN 24 HOURS)`
span.quote: RIFLE class is determined based on the worst of either glomerular filtration criteria or urine output criteria. Glomerular filtration criteria are calculated as an increase of serum creatinine above the baseline serum creatinine level. Acute kidney injury should be both abrupt (within 1–7 days) and sustained (more than 24 hours).

span.label: `acute kidney injury (renal-replacement sense)` - THE RIVAL DEFINITION THE PAPER NAMES: `our study highlights the potential for UNDER-REPORTING WHEN RENAL REPLACEMENT THERAPY IS USED TO 'DEFINE' ACUTE KIDNEY INJURY`. Under RIFLE 28% reach class F; only 14% of those are dialysed
span.quote: The incidence of almost 70% may appear at odds with the existing literature [ 5 ]. Even when limiting cases to those with RIFLE class F (28%) we found a higher rate for ICU patients than typically reported. Fourteen percent of class F patients received renal replacement therapy, however, leading to a rate of 4–5% among ICU patients, consistent with previous reports [ 9 , 19 ]. Indeed, our study highlights the potential for under-reporting when renal replacement therapy is used to 'define' acute kidney injury.

span.label: `baseline serum creatinine` - FOR ABOUT HALF THIS COHORT, NOT A MEASUREMENT: the MDRD equation solved backwards `ASSUMING a glomerular filtration rate of 75 ml/minute/1.73 m 2`, then the LOWEST of three candidate values taken
span.quote: For patients without chronic kidney insufficiency as reported in the medical history, we calculated a serum creatinine level using the MDRD equation [ 16 ] (Cr MDRD ) as recommended by the Acute Dialysis Quality Initiative, by solving the MDRD equation for serum creatinine assuming a glomerular filtration rate of 75 ml/minute/1.73 m 2 . We then used the lowest creatinine value among the hospital admission creatinine, the ICU admission creatinine or the Cr MDRD creatinine as the baseline value. Approximately one-half of patients were classified using the Cr MDRD as a baseline.

span.label: `class Failure` - reachable by a THIRD route when the baseline is already high: `When the baseline serum creatinine is elevated, AN ABRUPT RISE OF AT LEAST 0.5 mg/dl to more than 4 mg/dl IS ALL THAT IS REQUIRED to achieve class Failure`. A ratio rule with an absolute exception
span.quote: When the baseline serum creatinine is elevated, an abrupt rise of at least 0.5 mg/dl to more than 4 mg/dl is all that is required to achieve class Failure.

span.label: extends → the Acute Dialysis Quality Initiative's RIFLE consensus statement, which proposed the classification this study is the first to validate in a large general ICU cohort
span.quote: To establish a uniform definition for acute kidney injury, the Acute Dialysis Quality Initiative formulated the Risk, Injury, Failure, Loss, and End-stage Kidney (RIFLE) classification [ 11 ]. RIFLE defines three grades of increasing severity of acute kidney injury – risk (class R), injury (class I) and failure (class F) – and two outcome classes (loss and end-stage kidney disease)

span.label: contrasts-with → the literature that defines acute kidney injury by the need for renal replacement therapy, which the authors name as a source of under-reporting
span.quote: The incidence of almost 70% may appear at odds with the existing literature [ 5 ]. Even when limiting cases to those with RIFLE class F (28%) we found a higher rate for ICU patients than typically reported. Fourteen percent of class F patients received renal replacement therapy, however, leading to a rate of 4–5% among ICU patients, consistent with previous reports [ 9 , 19 ]. span.label: acute kidney injury —operationalised-as→ RIFLE classification
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.95 — `The RIFLE classification is a VERY SENSITIVE DEFINITION of acute kidney injury: acute kidney injury DEFINED BY the RIFLE classification occurred in TWO THIRDS of general ICU patients`. The definition's sensitivity is reported as a property of the definition, not of the patients
span.quote: The RIFLE classification is a very sensitive definition of acute kidney injury: acute kidney injury defined by the RIFLE classification occurred in two thirds of general ICU patients.

span.label: glomerular filtration rate criteria —distinct-from→ urine output criteria
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.95 — THE CLASSIFICATION TREATS THEM AS INTERCHANGEABLE BY CONSTRUCTION - a class is `the WORST OF EITHER` - AND THE OUTCOME DATA SAYS THEY ARE NOT: class F reached on creatinine carries 27.9% hospital mortality, class F reached on urine output 21.9%, P = 0.020. The authors add that `URINE OUTPUT AND CREATININE CRITERIA PROVIDE COMPLEMENTARY INFORMATION, WHICH IS LOST WHEN THESE CRITERIA ARE COMBINED`
span.quote: Patients with maximum RIFLE class F based on glomerular filtration rate criteria had a somewhat higher inhospital mortality compared with patients who had a maximum RIFLE class F on urine output criteria (27.9% versus 21.9%, P = 0.020).

span.label: Glomerular filtration criteria —operationalised-as→ baseline serum creatinine level
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.95 — `Glomerular filtration criteria are CALCULATED AS an increase of serum creatinine ABOVE THE BASELINE serum creatinine level` - so the whole arm is defined relative to a value that, for about half this cohort, was computed from an assumed glomerular filtration rate of 75 rather than measured

Glomerular filtration criteria are calculated as an increase of serum creatinine above the baseline serum creatinine level. Acute kidney injury should be both abrupt (within 1–7 days) and sustained (more than 24 hours).

span.quote: To establish a uniform definition for acute kidney injury, the Acute Dialysis Quality Initiative formulated the Risk, Injury, Failure, Loss, and End-stage Kidney (RIFLE) classification [ 11 ]. RIFLE defines three grades of increasing severity of acute kidney injury – risk (class R), injury (class I) and failure (class F) – and two outcome classes (loss and end-stage kidney disease)

span.label: `CALCULATED AS AN INCREASE OF SERUM CREATININE ABOVE THE BASELINE serum creatinine level`, with the injury required to be `both ABRUPT (WITHIN 1-7 DAYS) AND SUSTAINED (MORE THAN 24 HOURS)`
span.quote: RIFLE class is determined based on the worst of either glomerular filtration criteria or urine output criteria. Glomerular filtration criteria are calculated as an increase of serum creatinine above the baseline serum creatinine level. Acute kidney injury should be both abrupt (within 1–7 days) and sustained (more than 24 hours).

span.label: `When the baseline serum creatinine is elevated, AN ABRUPT RISE OF AT LEAST 0.5 mg/dl to more than 4 mg/dl IS ALL THAT IS REQUIRED to achieve class Failure` - an absolute exception inside a ratio rule

span.label: 75 — the glomerular filtration rate ASSUMED when solving the MDRD equation backwards to manufacture a baseline creatinine - used for about half the cohort
span.quote: For patients without chronic kidney insufficiency as reported in the medical history, we calculated a serum creatinine level using the MDRD equation [ 16 ] (Cr MDRD ) as recommended by the Acute Dialysis Quality Initiative, by solving the MDRD equation for serum creatinine assuming a glomerular filtration rate of 75 ml/minute/1.73 m 2 . We then used the lowest creatinine value among the hospital admission creatinine, the ICU admission creatinine or the Cr MDRD creatinine as the baseline value. Approximately one-half of patients were classified using the Cr MDRD as a baseline.

span.quote: The Acute Dialysis Quality Initiative recommended the use of a baseline serum creatinine, yet a true baseline is often unknown for patients admitted to the ICU. Our use of the lowest of these values for any given patient may have lead to a higher estimate of change and therefore a higher estimate of the incidence of acute kidney injury.
